citationSources.text: Maintenance testing: testing changes to a system that is already in operation, to keep it reliable and performing over time.

Corrective maintenance fixes defects found in operation. Adaptive maintenance adapts the system to a changed environment, such as a new operating system or database. Perfective maintenance improves performance or maintainability.

Triggers for maintenance testing: planned enhancements and releases, emergency fixes, upgrades or migrations of the operational environment, and retirement of the system, which may need data archiving tests.
Impact analysis identifies which parts of the system a change affects and how much regression testing is needed. It is harder when specifications are out of date or test cases are missing.
Maintenance releases may be planned or hot fixes. Regression tests should be automated where possible because they are repeated for every release.
Testing must fit the software development lifecycle: every development activity has a corresponding test activity, and test analysis and design start during the matching development activity.
In sequential models such as waterfall and the V-model, testing happens in phases; the V-model pairs each development level with a test level, for example requirements with acceptance testing.
In iterative and incremental models, each iteration delivers working software and includes static and dynamic testing at several levels; regression testing grows in importance with each increment.

Shift left means testing earlier: reviewing requirements, writing tests before code, running static analysis and continuous integration. It costs effort early but saves more later because early defects are cheaper to fix.
Retrospectives after an iteration or release capture what went well and what to improve, including test process improvements, and feed into the next cycle.
DevOps uses continuous integration and delivery pipelines; automated tests give fast feedback on every change, but manual exploratory testing is still needed.
Test levels are groups of test activities organised together: component testing, component integration testing, system testing, system integration testing and acceptance testing.
Component testing tests components in isolation, usually by developers, often with stubs and drivers. Component integration testing tests the interfaces and interactions between components.

System testing tests the whole system's behaviour and capabilities, including non-functional characteristics, often by an independent test team. System integration testing tests interfaces with other systems and external services.

Acceptance testing validates readiness for deployment and that the system meets users' business needs; forms include user acceptance, operational acceptance, contractual and regulatory acceptance, alpha and beta testing.

Test types: functional testing checks what the system does; non-functional testing checks how well it does it, such as performance, usability and security; black-box testing derives tests from the specification and white-box testing from the internal structure.
Confirmation testing checks that a reported defect has been fixed; regression testing checks that a change has not broken anything else.

citationSources.text: A defect report moves through a lifecycle. A tester finds a failure and logs a new defect report with steps to reproduce, expected and actual results, severity and environment.
The test lead reviews the new report. If it is a duplicate, it is closed as duplicate. If it cannot be reproduced, it goes back to the tester for more information.
A valid report is assigned to a developer, who analyses it. If the behaviour is intended, the report is rejected as not a defect, and the tester may reopen it with evidence.
Otherwise the developer fixes the defect and marks it fixed. The fix is deployed to the test environment.
The tester runs a confirmation test. If the defect still occurs, the report is reopened and goes back to the developer. If it passes, regression tests run on the affected area.
When confirmation and regression testing pass, the report is closed. Metrics such as defect age and reopen rate are collected for the retrospective.

messages.content: Show the defect lifecycle as a flowchart on the canvas.

rubric: Every state and decision in order; decision points visible with labelled branches (duplicate, cannot reproduce, rejected, reopened); loops shown; reads in one direction.

citationSources.text: Test process improvement often follows the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle.
Plan: set improvement goals from retrospectives and metrics, for example reducing escaped defects by a third, and choose the changes to try.
Do: apply the changes on a small scale, such as one team adopting test-first development for one release.
Check: measure the results against the goals using defect data and team feedback.
Act: adopt successful changes across teams, adjust or drop the rest, and feed the lessons into the next Plan step, so the cycle repeats.

messages.content: Make a diagram of this improvement cycle.

rubric: Four steps arranged as a cycle with arrows returning from Act to Plan; goal example kept; not a straight line or grid.

citationSources.text: Waterfall: phases run in sequence, requirements are fixed early, testing happens after implementation, so defects in requirements are found late and are expensive to fix. Suits stable, well-understood projects.
V-model: sequential like waterfall, but each development level has a matching test level planned in parallel, so test design starts early. Still poor at handling changing requirements.

Agile (iterative): short iterations deliver working software, testing is continuous within each iteration, requirements may change, and the whole team shares responsibility for quality. Needs strong automation for regression.
Choosing a model depends on how stable requirements are, regulatory needs, team size and how quickly feedback is needed.

rubric: The three models side by side with comparable points; differences easy to scan; the choosing factors kept; no invented criteria.

citationSources.text: Risk is the combination of the likelihood of a problem and its impact. Product risks concern the quality of the product; project risks concern the project's ability to deliver.
Risk-based testing uses risk analysis to decide what to test first, how deeply, and which techniques to use. Higher risk areas get more and earlier testing.
Risk analysis identifies risks, then assesses each by likelihood and impact, often on a matrix from low to high.
Mitigation reduces risk: testing reduces product risk by finding defects early. Some risks are accepted, transferred, or handled with contingency plans.
Risks are monitored throughout the project and the test plan is updated when they change.
